`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

## Self-review summary

I re-read the specification against my implementation and found one real correctness gap: costs are defined as arbitrary-length unsigned decimal integers with no bound, but I was using `parseInt`/plain JS numbers for cost, start, finish, priority, total, and makespan — which silently lose precision above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53). A hidden validator testing large costs would produce byte-mismatched output.

**Fix applied:** switched all cost-derived arithmetic to `BigInt` throughout:
- `parse.js` now stores `cost: BigInt(cost)` instead of `parseInt(cost, 10)`.
- `graph.js`'s `computeTimings`, `computePriorities`, `analyzeGraph`, and `packWorkers` now use `0n`/BigInt comparisons and arithmetic for `start`, `finish`, `depth`'s cost math, `priority`, `total`, worker `free` times, the simulation clock, and `makespan`. (`depth`, being a wave count rather than a cost sum, stays a plain number.)
- Fixed the `pack` tie-break comparator, which previously subtracted two BigInts and returned the result directly to `Array.prototype.sort` — that throws (`sort` calls `ToNumber` on the comparator's return value, and `ToNumber` on a BigInt is a `TypeError`). Replaced it with an explicit greater/less check that returns plain `-1/0/1`.
- Verified template-literal interpolation of BigInt values prints without the `n` suffix, so output formatting is unaffected.

I then re-verified every spec corner by hand: newline/comment/whitespace handling, name/cost character-set validation and error precedence, duplicate-declaration and unknown-directive detection, forward-referenced `dep` lines, the "first unknown name in input order" rule, self-loop and multi-node cycle detection with correct DFS ordering, empty-graph output for all three modes, zero-cost same-instant chaining in `pack`, worker-count validation (leading zero, zero, non-digit), usage-error precedence over stdin parsing, and now arbitrarily large costs for precision. All of these, plus the full visible suite (15/15 passing) and the `node_modules` absence check, are confirmed correct. Only files under `src/` were touched.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.
